newsitem.title: BURKINA FASO: Leaders gather for Franco-African summit.
newsitem.headline: Leaders gather for Franco-African summit.

text.p: Heads of state gathered on Wednesday for a Franco-African summit that was to focus on good governance in Africa but was overshadowed by conflict on the continent.
French President Jacques Chirac headed to the meeting in Ouagadogou despite a bombing in a Paris subway that killed two people and injured scores on Tuesday night.

Foreign ministers of about 20 African states with close ties to Paris met early on Wednesday to fine-tune the agenda for 30 heads of state who were meeting later in the day. The summits are held every two years, rotated between a French and African venue.
The ministers laboured for more than six hours on Tuesday night in the Burkina Faso capital to prepare resolutions on the main theme: good governance and development.
But turmoil in Central Africa looked certain to dominate, and ministers pointed in this direction by adopting a text reaffirming the inviolability of Africa's colonial borders, delegates said.
A notable absentee will be Zaire's President Mobutu sese Seko, Africa's longest serving head of state, in power for 31 years. Mobutu is in France recuperating from cancer surgery.
Turmoil in his vast Central African nation and its charges that neighbours are backing rebels who have seized a swathe of territory, look certain to be hotly debated at the meeting.
Rwanda and Uganda are virtually at war with Zaire and fierce fighting is raging in Burundi between government forces and Hutu rebels.

Further north, the Central African Republic is mired in its third army mutiny this year. Central African President Ange-Felix Patasse is missing the summit because of the two-week-old mutiny by soldiers in the capital demanding his resignation.
Patasse's spokesman Prosper Douba said on Tuesday that Patasse expected "heads of state of friendly countries to send delegations and commissions of inquiry" to Bangui to assess the situation.

"We are expecting the summit to examine the situation and the heads of state to make a decision on it and condemn what is going on, because we know that the rebels benefit from the support of a number of friendly forces who supply them with arms and ammunition," Douba said.
In several French-speaking states, military coups or revolts have undermined the democratic gains of the early 1990s.

France's influence in Africa faces a challenge from the United States, which last month vetoed U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's French-backed bid for a second term. He was the first U.N. head from Africa.
Delegates said the summit should come up with a Francophone African candidate after the Organisation of African Unity asked African states for nominees.

Ivory Coast's independent daily Le Jour headlined on Wednesday that Ivorian Foreign Minister Amara Essy was a candidate. Niger has already announced its intention to nominate Hamid Algabid, Secretary General of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference.
The meeting could set the stage for a hot contest for the U.N. job between French-speaking and English-speaking Africa.
